newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon steps up coffee, cocoa quality checks.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon steps up coffee, cocoa quality checks.

text.p: Cameroon, stung by customer complaints over cocoa and coffee quality after free-market reforms in the sector, has announced plans to tighten monitoring.
"All cocoa and coffee beans destined for export will be subjected to strict quality control measures," the government said in a decree just signed by Prime Minister Peter Musonge Mafany.
The National Cocoa and Coffee Board (NCCB) would emphasise checks by quality controllers certified by the ministry of trade and industry, it added.

Cameroon liberalised internal and external marketing in 1991 as part of donor-sponsored reforms, but a booming number of unregulated exporters and buyers put pressure on farmers to harvest crops earlier and skimp on fermenting and drying times.
Foreign buyers have complained about quality and handling, National Cocoa and Coffee Board (NCCB) director Hope Soan Ebai told Reuters.

Only three international chocolate firms had ventured into the produce sector in the past two years, he said, adding that Cameroon cocoa, which had traditionally attracted a premium for high butter-to-bean content, had lost its cachet.
European Union analyst Marc Litvine said good quality cocoa plunged from 76 percent of total exports in 1998/89 (Oct-Sept) to 17 percent in 1995/96.
Hauliers pointed to inadequate quality checks at port.

"At the port in Douala, whether the cocoa is good or bad, it is shipped," said one, adding that some exporters were also poorly equipped. "Here you can become an exporter without owning a storehouse," he said.
The NCCB relaxed its export monitoring role in 1991 and stopped providing guarantees for low-interest bank credits for exporters. Much of Cameroon's cocoa is now sold on a spot basis.
Ebai said in March that Cameroon aimed to regain the confidence of buyers and exporters so that forward sales, which once made up the bulk Cameroon's cocoa sales in the past, could be restored.
Coffee farmers say poor access to finance for hiring labour and treating crops encourages sloppy husbandry, harvesting and preparation for sale, leading to drops in output.
One told Reuters he had produced 233 tonnes of coffee from 200,000 coffee bushes in 1986/87. By the mid-1990s, output from his 20 hectares had dwindled to 50 tonnes.

"In the West Province, people rooted out their coffee after liberalisation and are now shifting to the production of groundnuts, which gives them far more revenue and less production cost," said Timothee Yimo, who is also vice-president of Cameroon's Interprofessional Council of Coffee and Cocoa.
Agriculture Minister Frederick Kodock said quality losses "had a disastrous effect on (Cameroon's) exports and balance of trade".
"Despite the annual increase of cocoa production from 109,000 tonnes in 1994/95 to 130,000 tonnes in 1995/96 quality fell drastically," he said after the decree.
Cameroon's 1996/97 cocoa harvest was estimated in March at 120,000 tonnes.
Yimo said coffee farmers needed state help.

"In 1995, Ivory Coast exported 180,000 tonnes of coffee while our production stood at 20,000 tonnes," he said. "The absence of support to those involved in the sector seems to be the major reason behind this poor quantity and quality."
A new mutual fund to guarantee export contracts was being considered, Ebai told Reuters in March.
